stem: A nurse is communicating with an alert client who has significant hearing impairment. Which approach is most appropriate?

options.A: Face the client in good lighting, reduce background noise, speak clearly at a natural, reasonable speed, and use a slightly louder voice without shouting.
options.B: Face the client in good lighting, shout the words, and intentionally over-enunciate instead of speaking naturally.
options.C: Keep the television on, turn away from the client while speaking, and use a faster pace to finish the interaction efficiently.
options.D: Look down at the chart while speaking at normal volume and avoid repeating or rewording information even when the client has difficulty understanding.

rationale: NIH National Institute on Aging guidance recommends finding a quiet place to reduce background noise, standing in good lighting, facing the person, speaking clearly, using a slightly louder voice without shouting, and speaking naturally at a reasonable speed. Therefore A is correct. B is incorrect because it uses shouting and over-enunciation rather than natural speech. C preserves background noise, removes face-to-face visual cues, and uses an unnecessarily fast pace. D removes facial/lip cues and withholds repetition or rewording even when understanding is difficult.
educational_objective: Select communication strategies for a client with hearing impairment that improve visual and auditory access without shouting or distorting natural speech.
source_organization: National Institutes of Health (NIH), National Institute on Aging (NIA)
source_document_title: Hearing Loss: A Common Problem for Older Adults
source_version_date: Content reviewed January 19, 2023; current NIH guidance as accessed 2026-08-16
source_locator: How to talk with someone who has hearing loss — quiet setting/reduced background noise; good lighting; face the person; speak clearly; slightly louder than normal without shouting; natural, reasonable speed; repeat/reword if necessary.
source_claim_supported: For hearing loss, improve communication by reducing background noise, using good lighting and face-to-face visual cues, speaking clearly at a natural reasonable speed, using a slightly louder voice without shouting, and repeating or rewording when needed.

source_original.stem: A nurse is communicating with an alert client who has significant hearing impairment. Which approach is most appropriate?

options.A: Face the client in good lighting, speak clearly at a normal volume and pace, and use written or other preferred communication methods when helpful.
options.B: Face the client but substantially increase volume and exaggerate mouth movements because louder, exaggerated speech improves understanding with hearing loss.
options.C: Speak from the client's better-hearing side while looking toward the chart because visual access to the speaker's face adds little when hearing is impaired.
options.D: Direct most questions to a companion and let the companion relay answers because hearing loss makes direct client communication less reliable.

source_original.rationale: Communication should be adapted to the client's hearing needs. Option A is correct because facing the client in good lighting, speaking clearly without shouting, and using preferred written or other methods can improve communication. Option B is incorrect because shouting and exaggerated speech can distort communication. Option C removes visual access to the speaker's face. Option D unnecessarily redirects communication away from the competent client.
source_original.source_detail: NCBI Bookshelf/Open RN Nursing Fundamentals, 2nd ed. (2024), Communication strategies for hearing impairment: face the client directly in good lighting, facilitate visual access, speak clearly without shouting/exaggeration, minimize background noise, and use the client's preferred written/assistive communication methods as needed. correction_summary: Rewrote the correct option and distractors to remove the weakly supported 'normal volume and pace' wording and unsupported distractor mechanisms; upgraded the clinical source to current official NIH/NIA guidance with an exact section locator while retaining the original construct and key A.

audit_findings.source_authority: Official NIH/NIA patient-communication guidance; NCSBN for blueprint
audit_findings.currentness: NIH page live and rechecked 2026-08-16; NCSBN 2026 plan current
audit_findings.exact_locator: NIH/NIA: How to talk with someone who has hearing loss; NCSBN page 11 Basic Care and Comfort sensory-impairment activity
audit_findings.claim_audit: All positive communication behaviors in A and rationale are directly supported by NIH/NIA; no unsupported dose, threshold, timing, or mechanism remains.

distractor_audit.B: Shouting and non-natural over-enunciation conflict with guidance.
distractor_audit.C: Background noise, turning away, and fast pacing conflict with guidance.
distractor_audit.D: Looking away removes visual cues; refusing repetition/rewording conflicts with guidance when understanding is difficult.

audit_findings.ambiguity_second_answer: Only A contains a fully recommended set of behaviors; B, C and D each contain direct conflicts with official guidance.
audit_findings.cueing: Options are comparable in length and all describe concrete communication behaviors.

audit_findings.independent_second_pass: Rechecked stem, all four options, rationale, objective, exact locators, blueprint mapping and second-answer risk from zero; A remained uniquely best.
